subject: Network handoff strategy for BrightEdge private deployment
messages:
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
To: Alex Moreno <alex@brightedge.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 29 Mar 2027 10:12:00 -0700
Subject: BrightEdge private deployment — handoff options and quick ask

Alex —

Thanks for the time on the call earlier. Per our conversation I wanted to summarize the three primary handoff patterns we typically recommend for Redwood Private (VPC / on-prem) customers and ask a couple quick questions so we can propose a recommended plan and timeline:

Options (short):
- VPC Peering: Low-latency, native intra-VPC routing. Requires reciprocal peering and some account-level trust; limited cross-account IAM control.
- AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints): Strong request-level access control and minimal routing exposure; uses NLBs/ENIs and supports per-service access lists.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec): Easiest to validate from customer's network policy perspective, supports static routes and NAT, but higher latency and operational overhead.

Quick asks for the recommendation:
1) Do you have a strict block on peering (org-level controls) or is peering allowed if we use a separate peering account?
2) Any requirement for fixed outbound IPs from Redwood to BrightEdge?
3) Target p95 latency for inference requests (ms) and expected RPS at peak.

Attached: rough topology diagram and a blank mutual action plan (brightedge_network_diagram.pdf). I can turn our suggested plan into a short canary + GA rollout once we have your constraints.

Suggested next step: 30-minute follow-up with your netops (cc'd) and Kimberly for security tradeoffs — are you available Wed/Thu this week?

Thanks,
Karthik
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

[attachment: brightedge_network_diagram.pdf]

From: Alex Moreno <alex@brightedge.com>
To: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
Cc: BrightEdge Network Team <netops@brightedge.com>
Date: Tue, 30 Mar 2027 09:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: BrightEdge private deployment — handoff options and quick ask

Karthik —

Thanks for the write-up and the diagram. A few constraints from our side:
- Peering at the account level is currently disallowed by our security policy (we do not permit long-lived peering with third parties).
- We require all inbound application traffic to land on a set of IPs behind our egress ACLs; ideally we’d like a predictable set of endpoints to allow in our firewall.
- No Internet Gateway exposure for service endpoints; all access must traverse our transit/vPN stacks.
- p95 latency target: <= 80ms for small payloads (short text generation), peak RPS 350 across regions — most traffic from us-east-1.

Given that, PrivateLink looks attractive because it gives us fine-grained control and keeps traffic in our VPC fabric. VPN is acceptable as a short-term pilot while we validate throughput and latency — but we'd prefer to avoid a permanent VPN if it increases operational burden.

I attached our network diagram (internal) showing the transit setup and egress ACLs.

—Alex
Head of Platform Engineering
BrightEdge Inc.

[attachment: brightedge_internal_transit_diagram.pdf]

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
To: Alex Moreno <alex@brightedge.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 1 Apr 2027 08:47:00 -0700
Subject: RE: BrightEdge private deployment — handoff options and quick ask

Alex / team —

Thanks for the constraints — that clarifies a lot. Quick assessment and recommendation from a security/ops perspective:

High level pros/cons (summary):
- PrivateLink (recommended):
  * Pros: No peering required, per-VPC ENI control, integrates with our service-level access lists, predictable ENI IP addresses for allowlisting (subject to AWS ENI churn; static NAT solutions available).
  * Cons: Requires NLB in front of the service; Small throughput/connection limits per ENI (we can scale NLBs), egress IP predictability requires NAT or managed egress. Potentially higher costs vs peering.

- Site-to-site VPN (pilot):
  * Pros: Easy to validate with your netops, predictable routing, straightforward allowlisting by source IP.
  * Cons: Higher encoder latency and jitter vs PrivateLink/peering, more ops (tunnel keepalive, rotation), single point per-tunnel bandwidth unless we run multiple tunnels.

- VPC Peering:
  * Pros: Lowest latency and simplest routing for high-throughput traffic.
  * Cons: Not an option given your org policy. Peering also conflates routing domains unless we use shared services account; still requires grant-level controls for tenant isolation.

Recommendation and proposed rollout:
1) Pilot with site-to-site VPN for 2 weeks to validate throughput and p95 latency with a sample traffic set. We’ll instrument with distributed tracing and token-level cost/latency breakdowns.
2) Parallel implementation of PrivateLink in a staging environment (create NLB + ENIs, verify TLS termination, scale NLB target groups). If PrivateLink meets p95 < 80ms at your peak RPS in staging, schedule a migration to PrivateLink for production.
3) For allowlisting: we propose to front PrivateLink endpoints with a small NAT fleet (Elastic IPs) so you can add static IPs to ACLs. This approach preserves your egress ACL model.
4) Mutual action plan deliverables: test plan (latency/RPS), security checklist (certs/KMS/LB config), rollout timeline.

Attachments: I exported a quick comparison spreadsheet and a sample MAP template (redwood-handoff-comparison.xlsx).

If you’re agreeable we can run the VPN pilot next week and I’ll kick off the PrivateLink staging work in parallel.

Kimberly Park
Director, Security & Deployments
Redwood Inference
